summary: Each step's rule rebuilds in a few lines of plain Python on lists and dictionaries (the best epoch from a history, dropout's mask and scaling, one change per run, the kept row, clipped noise, padded word ids), while nothing can run TensorFlow, NumPy, pandas or scikit-learn in the page, so no task trains or scores a real model.

steps.title: Part A, read first: the curves and the wrong examples, before changing anything
steps.reason: TensorFlow is not in the runtime, but History.history is a plain dictionary of lists, and finding the epoch of the lowest validation loss is a return value a check can read. The page names two mistakes a check catches: forgetting the + 1 that turns a position counting from 0 into an epoch, and reading the training list instead of its val_ twin.

steps.title: The levers: what each is for and the sign that says to pull it
steps.reason: The lever table is lookup, but dropout's rule is behaviour that runs in plain Python once the random mask is given as a list: dropped values become 0, kept ones are scaled by 1 / (1 - rate), and with training=False everything passes through. The page names forgetting the scaling and expecting dropout to act at predict time.

steps.title: One change at a time: measured on the same validation data
steps.reason: The rule that each run changes exactly one setting against the run before it, seed and validation rows included, shows up as a return value or a raised error over two settings dictionaries. The noise threshold and the test-set-once rule are judgements with no exact number on the page; if the trainer prefers them, a choice task on scoring the test set after every change fits instead.

steps.title: Worked example: one improvement on the digit network
steps.reason: Picking the kept model from the results table, the row with the lowest validation loss, is a return value over a list of dictionaries shaped like the page's results list. The page names picking by the test number and assuming the newest change is the kept one; the TFLearn keep_prob conversion is one subtraction, too small for a task of its own.

steps.title: When stuck: the symptom, its likely cause and the first check
steps.reason: Proposed by hand on 2026-11-20, after the step was added to the page (D-0104), and approved by the trainer in session. Three of the step's five error rows come from a loss that does not match the form of the labels or the output layer. The rule that pairs them is a small lookup with one special case, two classes, and each wrong pairing the table names fails a check.

steps.title: Part B, build 1: a denoising autoencoder
steps.reason: The model needs TensorFlow, but making the noisy input is plain arithmetic on a list of pixels with the noise passed in, drawn once: pixel plus 0.3 times noise, clipped to 0 to 1. The page's named mistakes, no clip and a noisy target (which an in-place change of the clean list produces), each fail a check.

steps.title: Part B, build 2: text with TextVectorization and Embedding
steps.reason: TextVectorization's output, a fixed-length list of word ids with 0 for padding and 1 for an unknown word, rebuilds in plain Python with split and a vocabulary list. The page and the brief name leaving output_sequence_length unset, so lengths do not match; the Embedding layer and what its vectors mean stay out, as the anti-spoiler row defers similarity to week 8.

tasks.title: Reading the curves
tasks.idea: The reader writes best_epoch(history), where history is a dictionary shaped like History.history with lists under "loss" and "val_loss", and returns the epoch, counting from 1, at which the validation loss is lowest. For a 20-epoch history whose smallest val_loss sits at position 11 it returns 12.
checks: A history whose lowest validation loss is at position 11 returns 12; an answer that leaves out the + 1 returns 11.
A history whose training loss falls for all 20 epochs while validation loss turns up after epoch 12 still returns 12; an answer that reads "loss" instead of "val_loss" returns 20.
tasks.q: Write best_epoch(history). history is a dictionary shaped like History.history: a list of numbers under "loss" for the training loss and one under "val_loss" for the validation loss, one number per epoch. Return the epoch at which the validation loss is lowest, counting epochs from 1, as the page's np.argmin(...) + 1 does. Plain Python is enough: min finds the smallest value and a list's index method gives its position, counting from 0. For a 20-epoch history whose smallest val_loss sits at position 11, best_epoch(history) returns 12.

tasks.title: Dropout
tasks.idea: The reader writes dropout(values, keep, rate, training): values is a list of numbers, keep a list of True or False of the same length standing in for the random draw, and the function returns a new list. With training true, a kept value is multiplied by 1 / (1 - rate) and a dropped one becomes 0.0; with training false the values come back unchanged. dropout([1.0, 1.0], [True, False], 0.2, True) returns [1.25, 0.0].
checks: With rate 0.2 and training true, kept ones come back as 1.25 and dropped ones as 0.0; an answer that zeroes the dropped values but does not scale the rest returns 1.0.
With training false the values come back unchanged even when keep holds False entries; an answer that applies the mask at predict time returns zeros.
With rate 0.5 a kept 3.0 comes back as 6.0; an answer that hard-codes the 1.25 from the page's example fails.
tasks.q: Write dropout(values, keep, rate, training), the rule a Dropout layer follows, on plain lists. values is a list of numbers and keep a list of True or False of the same length that stands in for the random draw: True means that value is kept. rate is the share dropped, as in Dropout(0.2). Return a list: with training true, each kept value is multiplied by 1 / (1 - rate) and each dropped one becomes 0.0; with training false, the values come back unchanged. For example dropout([1.0, 1.0], [True, False], 0.2, True) returns [1.25, 0.0].
tasks.tests:
assert dropout([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], [True, False, True], 0.2, True) == [1.25, 0.0, 1.25], "in training, kept values are scaled by 1 / (1 - rate) and dropped ones become 0.0"
assert dropout([1.0, 2.0], [False, False], 0.2, False) == [1.0, 2.0], "with training false every value comes back unchanged, whatever keep holds"
assert dropout([3.0, 3.0], [True, False], 0.5, True) == [6.0, 0.0], "the scale follows the rate: at 0.5 a kept 3.0 becomes 6.0"

tasks.title: One change at a time
tasks.idea: The reader writes the_one_change(before, after): two dictionaries of a run's settings with the same keys, such as "units", "dropout", "epochs", "seed" and "val_rows", and the function returns the name of the one setting that differs, or raises ValueError when none or more than one differs. With only "dropout" going from 0.0 to 0.2 it returns "dropout".
checks: Two runs that differ only in "dropout" return "dropout".
Two runs that differ in "units" and "dropout" raise ValueError, the page's case of a wider layer and dropout changed together; an answer that returns the first difference it finds fails.
Two runs that differ in "dropout" and "seed" raise ValueError; an answer that skips the seed as if it were not part of the comparison returns "dropout".
Two identical runs raise ValueError; an answer that returns None or an empty string when nothing changed fails.
tasks.q: Write the_one_change(before, after). Each argument is a dictionary of one run's settings, both with the same keys, such as "units", "dropout", "epochs", "seed" and "val_rows". Return the name of the one setting whose value differs between the two runs. When no setting differs, or more than one does, the comparison cannot say what moved the number, so raise ValueError. Every key counts, the seed and the validation rows included. For example, when only "dropout" goes from 0.0 to 0.2, it returns "dropout".

tasks.title: Choosing the kept model
tasks.idea: The reader writes kept_model(results), where results is a list of dictionaries shaped like the page's results table, each with "model", "val_loss" and "val_accuracy", and returns the "model" name of the row with the lowest validation loss. For the page's two rows it returns "dropout 0.2".
checks: When the lowest val_loss is in the first row of three, that row's name comes back; an answer that keeps the newest row, the last change tried, fails.
Rows that also carry a "test_accuracy" key are still chosen by val_loss; an answer that picks the best test number, the brief's pitfall of choosing on the test set, fails.
An answer that takes the largest val_loss instead of the smallest returns the worse model and fails the page's two-row table.
tasks.q: Write kept_model(results). results is a list of dictionaries shaped like the page's results table, one per trained model, each with a "model" name, a "val_loss" and a "val_accuracy"; a row may carry other keys as well. Return the "model" name of the row with the lowest validation loss, wherever that row sits in the list and whatever its other numbers say. For the page's two rows, base 20 epochs at a val_loss of 0.096 and dropout 0.2 at 0.065, it returns "dropout 0.2".
tasks.tests:
page_rows = [{"model": "base 20 epochs", "val_loss": 0.096, "val_accuracy": 0.979}, {"model": "dropout 0.2", "val_loss": 0.065, "val_accuracy": 0.984}]
three_rows = [{"model": "dropout 0.2", "val_loss": 0.065, "val_accuracy": 0.984}, {"model": "dropout 0.5", "val_loss": 0.071, "val_accuracy": 0.981}, {"model": "dropout 0.2, 256 units", "val_loss": 0.068, "val_accuracy": 0.983}]
with_test = [{"model": "base 20 epochs", "val_loss": 0.096, "val_accuracy": 0.979, "test_accuracy": 0.982}, {"model": "dropout 0.2", "val_loss": 0.065, "val_accuracy": 0.984, "test_accuracy": 0.980}]
assert kept_model(page_rows) == "dropout 0.2", "keeps the row with the lowest val_loss in the page's table"
assert kept_model(three_rows) == "dropout 0.2", "keeps the lowest val_loss even when it is the first row, not the newest"
assert kept_model(with_test) == "dropout 0.2", "chooses on val_loss even when another row's test number is higher"

tasks.title: Matching the loss to the labels
tasks.idea: The reader writes pick_loss(label_form, n_classes) and returns a tuple of the loss name, the number of output units and the output activation, following the week's builds: integer labels take sparse_categorical_crossentropy, one-hot labels take categorical_crossentropy, both with one softmax unit per class, and two classes with integer 0 and 1 labels take one sigmoid unit with binary_crossentropy.
checks: Integer labels over ten classes return the sparse loss with ten softmax units; an answer that swaps the sparse and the one-hot loss fails.
One-hot labels over three classes return categorical_crossentropy; an answer that always returns the sparse loss fails.
Integer labels over two classes return binary_crossentropy with one sigmoid unit; a one-unit softmax, the table's "always return the value 1" row, fails.
Integer labels over three classes return three units; an answer with the unit count fixed at ten fails.
tasks.q: Write pick_loss(label_form, n_classes). label_form is "integer" when each label is one whole number, or "one-hot" when each label is a row of zeros with a single 1. Return a tuple of three values: the loss name, the number of units in the output layer and its activation. Follow the week's builds. Integer labels take "sparse_categorical_crossentropy" and one-hot labels take "categorical_crossentropy", each with one "softmax" unit per class. The one special case is integer labels with two classes: they take "binary_crossentropy" with 1 unit and "sigmoid". For example, pick_loss("integer", 10) returns ("sparse_categorical_crossentropy", 10, "softmax").
tasks.tests:
assert pick_loss("integer", 10) == ("sparse_categorical_crossentropy", 10, "softmax"), "integer labels over ten classes take the sparse loss and ten softmax units"
assert pick_loss("one-hot", 3) == ("categorical_crossentropy", 3, "softmax"), "one-hot labels take categorical_crossentropy"
assert pick_loss("integer", 2) == ("binary_crossentropy", 1, "sigmoid"), "two classes with 0 and 1 labels take one sigmoid unit and binary_crossentropy"
assert pick_loss("integer", 3) == ("sparse_categorical_crossentropy", 3, "softmax"), "the unit count follows the number of classes"

tasks.title: Noisy input, clean target
tasks.idea: The reader writes add_noise(pixels, noise, scale=0.3): pixels is a list of values between 0 and 1, noise a list of numbers of the same length drawn once beforehand, and the function returns a new list with each pixel plus scale times its noise, clipped to 0.0 at the bottom and 1.0 at the top. add_noise([0.9, 0.1, 0.5], [1.0, -1.0, 0.0]) returns [1.0, 0.0, 0.5].
checks: A sum above 1 comes back as 1.0 and a sum below 0 as 0.0; an answer without the clip returns 1.2 and -0.2.
A sum that stays inside 0 to 1 comes back as pixel plus scale times noise; an answer that adds the noise without the scale fails.
The caller's pixels list is left as it was, so the clean target survives; an answer that writes the noise into it in place leaves both arrays noisy, as fit(x_noisy, x_noisy) would.
tasks.q: Write add_noise(pixels, noise, scale=0.3), the noisy input of a denoising autoencoder, on plain lists. pixels is a list of pixel values between 0 and 1, and noise a list of numbers of the same length, drawn once beforehand. Return a new list in which each pixel becomes the pixel plus scale times its noise, clipped to 0.0 at the bottom and 1.0 at the top, as np.clip(x, 0.0, 1.0) does. Leave pixels itself as it was: it is the clean target. For example add_noise([0.9, 0.1, 0.5], [1.0, -1.0, 0.0]) returns [1.0, 0.0, 0.5].
tasks.tests:
assert add_noise([0.9, 0.1], [1.0, -1.0]) == [1.0, 0.0], "clips a sum above 1 to 1.0 and a sum below 0 to 0.0"
assert [round(p, 6) for p in add_noise([0.5, 0.2], [1.0, 1.0]) + add_noise([0.25], [0.5], 0.5)] == [0.8, 0.5, 0.5], "a sum inside 0 to 1 is the pixel plus scale times its noise"
clean = [0.5, 0.9]
noisy = add_noise(clean, [1.0, 1.0])
assert clean == [0.5, 0.9], "leaves the caller's pixels list as it was, so the clean target survives"

tasks.title: Text to word ids
tasks.idea: The reader writes to_ids(text, vocabulary, length): vocabulary is a list that starts with "" and "[UNK]", the text is split on spaces, and the function returns exactly length ids, each word's position in the vocabulary, 1 for a word not in it, padded with 0 at the end or cut to length. With vocabulary ["", "[UNK]", "the", "bike", "car"], to_ids("the bike hit the car", vocabulary, 7) returns [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 0, 0].
checks: A post shorter than length is padded with 0 up to length; an answer that returns only the words' ids, as an unset output_sequence_length would, comes back too short.
A post longer than length is cut to its first length ids; an answer that only pads returns a list too long.
A word missing from the vocabulary becomes 1, the [UNK] id; an answer that drops the word or lets vocabulary.index raise ValueError fails.
A known word becomes its position in the vocabulary, so "the" is 2; an answer that counts positions from 1 or skips the two reserved entries is off.
tasks.q: Write to_ids(text, vocabulary, length), what TextVectorization does to one post once it has a vocabulary. vocabulary is a list whose first two entries are the reserved "" (padding, id 0) and "[UNK]" (an unknown word, id 1). Split text on spaces and turn each word into its id: its position in vocabulary, or 1 for a word not in it. Return exactly length ids, as output_sequence_length sets: a shorter post is padded with 0 at the end and a longer one is cut to its first length ids. With vocabulary = ["", "[UNK]", "the", "bike", "car"], to_ids("the bike hit the car", vocabulary, 7) returns [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 0, 0].
tasks.tests:
vocabulary = ["", "[UNK]", "the", "bike", "car"]
assert to_ids("the bike", vocabulary, 5) == [2, 3, 0, 0, 0], "pads a short post with 0 up to length"
assert to_ids("the car the bike the car", vocabulary, 4) == [2, 4, 2, 3], "cuts a long post to its first length ids"
assert to_ids("the bike hit the car", vocabulary, 7) == [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 0, 0], "turns a word missing from the vocabulary into 1, the [UNK] id"
assert to_ids("car bike the", vocabulary, 3) == [4, 3, 2], "gives a known word its position in the vocabulary, counting the two reserved entries"
